projectOutComesReport:
The behavior of materials in the deep Earth constrains the flows that drive plate tectonics. Voluminous volcanic eruptions driven by deep mantle sources are thought to have caused global environmental changes. At the core-mantle boundary -  about 3000 km below the Earth's surface - dramatic compositional and thermal changes occur, influencing the cooling of the planet and core dynamics (hence Earth's magnetic field). Indeed, multidisciplinary efforts and state-of-the art techniques are required to tackle the complex Earth system. With our individual expertise in seismology (Zhan), geodynamics (Gurnis), and experimental mineral physics (Jackson), we have connected the atomic scale to the tectonic scale, while linking processes to the temporal dimension through reconstruction of tectonic plate history. The fundamental questions we have addressed include: How do subducted slabs interact and affect chemically-distinct structures near the edges of Large Low Seismic Velocity Provinces (LLSVPs)? If hydrous phases can be transported into the lower mantle, are they seismically detectable, and if so, at what length scale? Is iron-rich (Mg,Fe)O a source of observable seismic anisotropy in ultralow velocity zones, developed by mantle flow near paleo-slabs?

Beyond scientific findings, the principal goals and impacts of this effort have been the cross-training of young scientists in a multidisciplinary collaborative framework (7 graduate students - including 3 Caltech PhD Dissertations, 5 postdoctoral scholars, and 3 undergraduate/high-school students, half of whom are women). The students, postdocs, and PIs published at least 17 papers in peer-reviewed literature and presented roughly 25 abstracts at scientific conferences and workshops, with highlights summarized here.

Slabs, scattering, and "water" in the mantle:

We applied our inter-source interferometry technique to probe small-scale intra-slab heterogeneity in the mantle transition zone beneath the Japan Sea to understand the chemistry of slab cores by analyzing the scattering content of seismograms. The observed weakening of scattering strength reveals that the dehydration process of the slab core must be complete by 410 km and could possibly lead to (re-)hydration of the slab crust (Shen et al. 2021), a process that could resume the visibility of seismic scatterers at the base of the transition zone. A systematic analysis of the origin of short-wavelength (<10 km) scatterers at 660 km depth, using synthetic seismograms at high frequencies computed on high resolution subduction and long term mixing models coupled with thermodynamics, shows that the origin of the short-wavelength scatters are neither likely from the complex phase transition in the subduction zone, nor from long-term mechanical mixing in the mantle (the traditional model for the origin of seismic scatters in the mantle). Instead, the origin might be intrinsic heterogeneities inside the subducted oceanic lithosphere (Mao et al. 2022), possibly leading to dense oxyhydroxide phase-formation.

The link between water activity in the lower mantle and the spin crossover of ferric iron in dense oxyhydroxide δ-(Al, Fe3+)OOH has been demonstrated, suggesting increased stability of dense oxyhydroxides throughout most of the lower mantle (Buchen et al. 2021; Buchen et al. 2023, under review). We further show that bulk sound speed and shear wave speed anomalies observed at the boundaries of LLSVPs can be produced by 7-12 vol.% δ-(Al,Fe3+)OOH, suggesting that phases in the (Al,Fe3+)OOH-MgSiO2(OH)2 system may also exhibit these properties (Ohira et al. 2021; Strozewski et al. 2023). Accumulation of dense hydrous phases therefore provides a plausible explanation for observed seismic anomalies near LLSVPs.

Underneath the Pacific Plate:

The Large Low Seismic Velocity Provinces (LLSVPs), one of the most significant features above the core-mantle boundary (CMB), are critical for understanding the nature of mantle convection and the evolution of Earth's interior but remain enigmatic. Seismic waveform modeling shows sharp, steep, and tilting boundaries of the Pacific LLSVP and the eastern side of the African LLSVP. We have investigated the tilting angle of LLSVPs' boundary (θ) by running a series of computational models with variable, but high bulk modulus (K) and high density (ρ) in the presence of paleo-slabs in the lower mantle. The outward tilting phenomenon is directly related to the density contrast within the pile as well as between the pile and the slab. Maximum tilting angle is generally linearly decreasing with increasing δρ. Large δK could increase chemical pile stability.

At the mantle base and underneath present day Hawaiʻi, seismic waves sampling the northeastern edge of the Pacific LLSVP show strong waveform complexity and rapid changes in differential time. We integrate constraints from seismic observations, mineral physics, and geodynamic simulations to provide best-fit phase assemblages that strongly support a solid-state ultralow velocity zone (ULVZ) interpretation featuring iron-rich (Mg,Fe)O magnesiowuestite (Lai et al. 2022), where ULVZs could exhibit seismic anisotropy (Jackson and Thomas 2021). Using a dual-technique approach to constrain the melting curve of FeO at CMB conditions, we find that FeO remains a solid at current CMB temperatures, providing strong evidence for magnesiowuestite-bearing ULVZs (Dobrosavljevic et al. 2023, under review).

abstractText:
Understanding the structure of the set of rational points on an elliptic curve (essentially a cubic equation) has been an aim in number theory for over a century. It has connections to open problems (such as the congruent number problem) buried in antiquity. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer (BSD) conjecture predicts a mystifying relation among the rational points and the associated L-function. The intriguing L-functions appear in various areas of mathematics and also in physics. Even though analytic in appearance, the L-functions reveal striking affinity to arithmetic.

The PI seeks to study certain arithmetic aspects of special values of L-functions. The first part of the project aims to establish a p-adic criterion for an elliptic curve to have analytic rank (the vanishing order of the associated L-function at its center) one. It will build on the recent progress towards the BSD conjecture (due to Skinner, Zhang and others) and aims to remove some of the key hypotheses. The other part of the project aims to study mod p non-vanishing of special values of L-functions in vertical and horizontal families. It will build on the progress during the last two decades (due to Hida, Michel--Venkatesh and others).

abstractText:
Non Technical:
This project aims to explore the electronic properties of engineered materials that are assembled one atomic layer at a time, starting from individual sheets of graphene and certain semiconductors, so-called transition metal dichalcogenides. For precise well-defined rotational misalignment angle between the layers, electrons in these materials strongly interact which leads to the emergence of correlated quantum electronic phases. The research team will image these emerging phases using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy techniques in various geometries. This approach will allow the team to gain insights into how the microscopic properties of correlated phases relate to their overall transport signatures. This information can be used to develop novel electronic quantum devices. The team will disseminate the project results through international conferences, journal articles, invited talks, publicly available blog posts, and educational videos targeting a broad audience. Besides the research component, this project aims to provide ample opportunities for integrating undergraduate education and increasing diversity through summer internships and programs for underrepresented minorities and outreach activities targeting high-school students and teachers from the Pasadena School District. 

Technical:
The discovery of layered quasi-two-dimensional crystals enabled a new way of designing tunable electronic systems in which electron-electron interactions are controlled through the rotational alignment (twist) of the stacked layers. The focus of this project is to explore properties of emerging correlated quantum electronic phases, including superconductivity and orbital ferromagnetism, in twisted multi-layer graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides heterostructures. One of the main goals is to establish a basic understanding of underlying symmetries and symmetry breaking phenomena that occur in these emerging phases using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy and by studying heterostructures in gate-tunable multi-terminal geometries. This research project is accompanied by an extensive mentoring and outreach plan aimed to prepare graduate and undergraduate students for successful careers in science and industry and help educate the public about quantum science and nanotechnology.

projectOutComesReport:
This project advanced the understanding of strongly correlated phases in van der Waals heterostructures based on rotationally misaligned graphene multilayers. Besides their fundamental importance, understanding symmetry-breaking mechanisms and residual symmetries in this family of materials holds promise for identifying key ingredients for the emergence of various superconducting and topological phases. The primary scientific outcomes of this award are listed in the following: 

(i) In twisted graphene bilayers, we have deepened the understanding of how symmetry breaking arises as the twist angle approaches the magic-angle value. We have established that the so-called Hartree correction, a consequence of non-uniform charge distribution in this material, effectively leads to the flattening of the electronic bands, thus enhancing correlation effects. This enhancement is robust in a larger angle range than anticipated from the simple continuum model. Ultimately, it leads to the breaking of internal four-fold spin-valley degeneracy and the formation of topological bands with non-zero Chern numbers. 


(ii) In a separate line of efforts, we have studied the relation between symmetry breaking and superconductivity in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene. Besides establishing spectroscopic signatures of unconventional superconductivity in this system, we have determined that both superconductivity and correlated insulating states emerge from the so-called inter-valley coherent parent normal state in which electrons from the opposite valleys are coherently mixed. This mixing is characterized by the distinct local density of state signatures that emerge on the graphene atomic lattice length scale. The parent state is more precisely identified as an incommensurate Kekulé spiral state by observing additional real space modulation on the Moiré length scales. Combined, these observations directly suggest that the inter-valley coherence is essential for forming correlated superconductivity in this system.  


Regarding broader impacts, this award helped support several training opportunities for undergraduates and various outreach activities involving visiting high school students.

abstractText:
The development of renewable alternatives to fossil fuel-based energy is one of the most critical scientific challenges of the United States. Electrocatalysis is a cornerstone to bridging renewable electrical energy resources (solar, hydro, and wind power, etc.) with chemical transformations central to energy storage and conversion. The project will develop an emerging class of electrocatalytic materials to maximize the efficiency of hydrogen fuel production from water. The outcome of this project makes a major contribution to hydrogen fuel technology development and supports the nation’s efforts to diversify energy supply and reduce the dependence on non-renewable energy sources. The knowledge generated from this project will advance general understanding and research in catalysis and other technologies, including batteries and sensors. The research is supplemented by a range of educational and outreach activities primarily for K-12 and undergraduate students from underrepresented groups to increase their interest in careers as scientists and engineers.

This project represents a cross-disciplinary and cross-institute effort to develop well-defined single atom catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) - the key barrier reaction for water electrolyzer and renewable hydrogen production. The project integrates the co-investigators' respective expertise in experimental and computational catalysis to address three questions paramount to OER catalysis: how to identify or construct well-defined catalytic centers for OER; how to delineate unambiguously the atomistic mechanism for OER at this center; and how to leverage the mechanistic understanding and the synthetic technique to fine-tune catalytic centers for optimal kinetics.  The primary strategy is to computationally design and precisely synthesize single-atom catalytic centers (e.g. cobalt) in the surface of well-defined and chemically stable metal oxide nanocrystals, thereby optimizing the OER performance through mechanistic understanding and synthetic modulation. Three specific tasks are included: (1) synthesizing cobalt single-atom catalytic centers with diverse and controllable metal oxide phase, composition, and surface facets; (2) understanding dependence of the reaction mechanism and kinetics on composition and atomic structure through a combination of computational and experimental approaches; and (3) using this understanding to conduct in silico scanning of reasonable compositions, combined with Machine Learning based on the validated computational model, followed by experimental synthesis of the predicted best candidates to identify the optimal single-atom and metal oxide compositions. Educational outreach involves the participation of undergraduate and K-12 students in summer research internships in the investigators’ laboratories as well as visits by the investigators and graduate students to the minority-serving partner institutions to deliver short courses based on their research.

projectOutComesReport:
One major goal was to develop new computational methods to predict accurately the rates and products of electrocatalytic reactions as a function of applied potential and to validate the accuracy by comparing to experiments by Prof. Sen Zhang of U. Virginia on Single Crystal nanocatalysts and on nanomaterials and to other experiments with a focus on

  • The oxygen evolution reaction (OER),
  • The Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER),
  • The N2 reduction reaction (N2RR) to NH3, and
  • The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) critical for hydrogen fuel cells

The second major goal was to apply these now validated new methods to in silico prediction of new electrocatalysts, ranking them, and selecting only the best to be tested experimentally.

Highlights of accomplishments 

1. Grand Canonical Potential Kinetics (GCP-K), We developed and validated a new computation technology, the Grand Canonical Potential Kinetics (GCP-K), or GC-QM, that leads to accurate free energy reaction barriers and energetics for all the steps of OER, HER, N2RR, and ORR under the conditions of electrocatalyst experiments.

Here exactly the same potential is applied to all reaction steps (9 for OER), including the reaction transition states. Normal QM has a fixed number of electrons, so that the potential changes between initial state, transition state, and final state; hence it cannot be used for electrocatalysis. With GC-QM the transition state geometry is allowed to change adiabatically as the applied potential is changed. Thus, we can predict which applied potential gives the optimum production of the desired products. GC-QM now enables theory to predict changes in transition state structure and free energy barrier as a function of potential directly from QM.

We have applied GC-QM to all four electrocatalytic processes listed above.

2. Validation of the accuracy of GC-QM for OER on Co/TiO2 single crystal nanoparticles (with Sen Zhang, U. Virginia)

The most important validation was on the Co/TiO2 single crystal nanoparticles prepared by Sen Zhang. We have predicted OER for many electrocatalysts but the validation with experiment has been difficult because the actual surface structure is almost never known from the experiment. However, Zhang prepared Co/TiO2 single crystal nanoparticles, for which the surface facets are all the same. The predicted free energies for all 9 steps of the OER on Co/TiO2 are shown in Figure 1 for applied potentials of 1.4 to 1.6 V. Figure 2 (right side) compares the predicted rate per surface site (TOF) with experiment, showing excellent agreement. The theory leads to currents about 25% larger than experiment, implying that the predicted transition state barrier is too low by only 0.03 eV! Figure 3 compares the current as a function of potential, making this new OER catalyst a substantial improvement over current generation OER catalysts.

3. validation for HER on WSe2 and WTe2 single layer electrocatalyst.

Chalcogenides such as WSe2 and WTe2 are layered making it possible to experimentally study the electrochemistry at the basal plane surface, so the surface structure is known for the theory. Figure 4 shows the GC-QM predicted current versus applied potential for the HER on WSe2 and WTe2, leading to onset potentials within ~ 0.05 V with experiment, a second very clean validation of GC-QM. Now we can use GC-QM to predict the performance numerous new potential electrocatalysts for OER, HER, N2RR, and ORR, enabling the experiments to focus only on the best predicted candidates.

4. HER rates on low index facets versus edges of Pt

Pt has long served as the gold standard for HER, but surprisingly there remains considerable uncertainty in the role played by step edges compared to the prominent facets. In collaboration with experimentalist Xiangfeng Duan at UCLA using ~1.5 nm diameter Pt nanowires (NW), we have made a major advance in showing that the edges lead to rates >100 times faster than the facets. This suggests that Pt catalysts might be made 10 or 100 times more active by optimizing edge concentrations.

Figures 5 and 6 summarize our results. In order to describe the water environment around the NW, we use 3061 water molecules, 60 H3O+, plus the Pt NW for over 10,000 atoms in a periodic box. This is far too large for QM (limited to <300 atoms and <100 ps for practical calculations), thus we used the ReaxFF reactive force field, trained to reproduce reaction trajectories from QM MD, but practical for systems with millions of atoms (cited >5300 times). Fig. 6c shows that the transition state free energies are substantially lower for edges. The result is that the edge rates (TOF) are > 100 faster than the facet rates (Fig. 6e), suggesting that rates measured on facets are probably dominated by the few percent edges present.

abstractText:
Molecules with ring structures are found in everything from drugs to plastics, where their special structures confer important functional properties. The bottleneck for discovering and developing such molecules and materials is often a limited ability to build complex rings from simple starting materials. This project establishes powerful and generalizable enzymatic routes to diverse ring structures, using chemistry not previously known in biological catalysis. The new-to-nature ring-forming enzymes are entirely genetically encoded, use earth-abundant iron, and function under mild conditions for sustainable production of a variety of materials, pharmaceuticals and chemicals. This interdisciplinary project trains highly talented graduate students and postdoctoral fellows for academic and industrial research in sustainable chemistry, biotechnology, and bioengineering. It is intended to inspire development of new catalyst technologies and methods for enzyme discovery and engineering.

This research builds on the principal investigator’s successful engineering of hemeproteins for new-to-nature carbene and nitrene transfer reactions and extends it to discovery and optimization by directed evolution of new enzyme catalysts. These catalysts are used for preparing ring structures that are difficult to make using synthetic chemistry. Intramolecular carbene and nitrene C–H insertion reactions are optimized to access important ring-containing molecules such as lactams, lactones and cyclic amines. In many cases there are no equivalent small-molecule catalysts for these transformations, therefore they will be enabled catalytically for the first time. The utility of the evolved biocatalysts is evaluated in synthesis and late-stage modification of bioactive molecules and precursors to advanced materials. This research also includes kinetic, spectroscopic, structural and computational studies to elucidate the mechanisms of the enzymatic ring-forming reactions and support further enzyme engineering or development of small-molecule catalyst counterparts.

This project is co-funded by the Systems and Synthetic Biology cluster in the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences, the Cellular and Biochemical Engineering program in the Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental, and Transport Systems and the Chemistry of Life Processes program in the Division of Chemistry.

projectOutComesReport:
With this grant, we were able to generate useful enzymes that can transform relatively simple chemicals into complex ring structures often found in natural products and pharmaceuticals. These enzymes make highly specific chiral products that are difficult or even impossible to make directly using chemical methods. These enzymes expand the repertoire of DNA-encoded chemistry to entirely new transformations and open the route to discovery of many more.  This research also improved our mechanistic understanding of these new-to-nature reactivities and demonstrated different strategies for developing new catalysts.

Intellectual Merit

A major early achievement was construction of chiral, 5- and 6-membered lactones through an intramolecular, benzylic carbene C-H insertion reaction catalyzed by engineered heme proteins known as cytochrome P450s. This reaction was extended to 7-membered rings, related allylic substrates, and to constructing complex ring systems including fused, spiro, and bridged rings (illustrated in Figure 1). Some of these products just cannot be made using chemical approaches. The transformation was also extended to building non-lactone structures, including a 5-membered cyclic ketone and a γ-lactam (obtained without protection/deprotection steps on nitrogen).

This grant also allowed us to develop catalysts for making cyclic amines using nitrene C-H insertion chemistry. The platform of enzymes, engineered using directed evolution, was active against a broad array of alkyl and aryl azides, forming products in good yields and high enantioselectivities, including at preparative scale (mmol). (Figure 2)  The scope of cyclic amine synthesis was further developed to include challenging substrates with unactivated C(sp3)-H bonds, albeit with low initial yields (2-3%). Promising activity that can be evolved further was observed with a 2,5-difluoro substrate to prepare a building block for the drug larotrectinib. This enzymatic platform has been further expanded to enable alkyl nitrene transfer reactions, unlocking novel routes to valuable N-heterocycles like piperidines and pyrrolidines, which are highly prevalent in pharmaceuticals.

Cyclopropanation of terminal alkenes with trifluorodiazoethane was developed and demonstrated on a broad range of olefins, producing products that had not been previously synthesized and successfully producing quaternary chiral centers. Computational studies analyzed the origins of cis/trans selectivity.

Studying the mechanism of carbene transfer catalysis in a newly evolved enzyme that can transfer diazoacetonitrile to mixtures of highly similar alkenes to form a cyclopropane and a ring-opened alkylation product showed that one particular (Z) isomer of the alkene selectively formed the cyclopropane while the other (E) isomer selectively formed the alkylation product, both with >99% chemoselectivity. Both products had an S configuration, implying a common intermediate and a stepwise pathway for enzymatic carbene transfer, in contrast to most reported concerted mechanisms.   

Progress in studying the mechanism of carbene transfer catalysis also enabled rational engineering of a cytochrome c for carbon-silicon bond formation via carbene insertion into Si-H bonds, showing high chemoselectivity over the alternative C-N bond formation, which is preferred when using chemical catalysts. Computational and experimental tools established that controlling loop conformation altered the protein's chemoselectivity from silylation to amination. This work demonstrated how structural information and dynamics, combined with mechanistic knowledge, enable selective non-natural transformations (Figure 3).

Finally, a computational approach enabled access to enantioselective carbene N-H bond insertions. Molecular dynamics simulations allowed us to identify mutations that reverse selectivity for forming different product enantiomers (compounds that have left- or right-handed versions), something that is extremely difficult or even impossible to do with chemical catalysts. The evolved enzymes accepted a broad scope of amine substrates with excellent yields (up to >99%), high efficiency (up to 12,300 TTN), and good control over the enantioselectivity for both versions of the product.  

Broader Impacts

Enzymes are remarkable catalysts with great promise for lowering the production costs of complex chemicals, such as pharmaceuticals (which often generate huge amounts of waste products, often 100 times as much as the weight of the pharmaceutical product).  Enzymes can often greatly reduce the number of steps needed to make a chemical, because they can catalyze transformations with high selectivity -- that is, they make a single product, even though many are possible.  Furthermore, the reactions they catalyze and their selectivities are evolvable.  This work shows that enzymes can be evolved to catalyze reactions previously unknown in nature, and that the selectivities and activities of these reactions can be evolved to generate catalysts that are highly useful and could be used to replace current chemical synthesis methods.  Our work has demonstrated different strategies that can be used for engineering novel biocatalysts.

abstractText:
This project is a multi-year research plan to develop new tools for the study of the structure of transformation groups and mapping class groups. The transformation groups such as diffeomorphism groups and homeomorphism groups of a manifold describe all symmetries of the manifold. A manifold is a space that is locally a Euclidean space. The surface of the earth, the surface of a donut and our three or four dimensional universe are all examples of manifolds. The mapping class group is a reduced form of the homeomorphism group of a manifold, in which two transformations are identified if they can be connected by a path of transformations.  These objects have connections with many areas of mathematics, including geometric topology, geometric group theory, dynamics, number theory, quantum field theory, representation theory, and algebraic geometry. This project studies a number of questions about the structure of symmetries of manifolds.  Broader impacts of these efforts include reading groups for graduate students. 

Previously, in a joint work with Kathryn Mann, the principal investigator has proved Ghys' dimension conjecture that given two manifolds M and N, if the homeomorphism group of M has a nontrivial homomorphism to the homeomorphism group of N, then the dimension of M must be less than or equal to the dimension of N. To prove this, an "Orbit Classification Theorem" is developed, which says that every orbit of such a homomorphism is homeomorphic to a cover of some configuration space of M. This finding has a potential to give more results about classifying homomorphisms between transformation groups. Since we have figured out all orbits, now the challenge is to understand how to glue those orbits inside the manifold N.  Another line of work studies the projection map from the transformation group to the mapping class group. In particular, we ask which subgroups of the mapping class group have sections under the projection, where the existence of sections implies that the surface bundle that the subgroup determines will admit a flat structure. In previous work on this subgroup question the principal investigator has proved several results using techniques of "hidden torsion" and rotation number. More tools will be developed specifically to attack this question. Another direction to explore concerns diffeomorphism groups of high dimensional manifolds, specifically, whether there is an example of an infinite torsion group that acts faithfully on some manifold.

abstractText:
Accurate measurements of wind speeds are crucial for many engineering applications, including wind energy, weather forecasting, drone navigation, and mitigation of dangers such as air pollution, wildfires, and airborne pathogens. Most wind-measuring devices used today are fixed in space and have high deployment costs. However, the built environment is already naturally instrumented with a variety of structures that move in response to the wind, from swaying trees to flapping flags. The principal aim of this project is to develop a physics-based understanding of those flow-structure interactions and to combine that knowledge with machine learning techniques to achieve unprecedented wind measurement capabilities. The project will incorporate laboratory measurements of vegetation exposed to controlled wind conditions in a large wind tunnel, and also field measurements in naturally occurring winds. K-12 engagement will be facilitated by emphasizing the timely applications of this research, especially firefighting and pollution monitoring, both of which are pressing challenges in southern California where the students live. 

An initial proof-of-concept has demonstrated the feasibility of using visual measurements of flow-structure interactions of vegetation to resolve wind speeds using a neural network. The goal of this project is to enable generalization beyond the initial training data set by incorporating a physics-based understanding of flow-structure interactions into the network architecture. The first objective is to determine which physical properties of the flow-structure interaction can be extracted by the model and are necessary for accurate wind speed predictions. Then, a broader training set and physics-based constraints will enable wind speed inference from classes of vegetation not used to train the model. A formal post hoc analysis of the neural network will further elucidate the salient flow physics. This project can improve the physical understanding of flow-structure interactions through development and subsequent analysis of the physics-based, machine learning approach to visual anemometry. The physical insights that will be gained from the data-driven approach will be considered along with a purely physics-based, first-principles approach to generalize the model and better understand its limitations. Moreover, because physics-informed machine learning is of broad interest in basic research, the approach to visual anemometry in this project can provide a template for similar efforts toward other research questions. A main outcome of this project, in addition to new knowledge regarding fluid dynamics and development of physics-informed machine learning, will be creation of a robust, quantitative visual anemometry technique.

projectOutComesReport:
This research project presents a significant advancement in wind speed measurement through the development of a novel technique termed visual anemometry. Traditional anemometry relies on intrusive instruments that can disrupt the very flow they aim to quantify, additionally suffering from limitations in providing only point or line measurements. Visual anemometry offers a more elegant solution by leveraging a single camera to observe vegetation sway and infer a comprehensive wind speed map across the field of view.

The core of this success lies in a newly developed model that utilizes the concept of the Reynolds number. This dimensionless parameter incorporates wind speed, a characteristic length scale, and fluid properties to predict the response of the canopy to wind forces. To validate this model, meticulous data collection was undertaken from a diverse range of plant species within controlled laboratory settings and real-world field environments. The results demonstrate exceptional efficacy, with our model achieving wind speed predictions comparable to existing methods that still necessitate traditional anemometers for reference.

Critically, this approach eliminates the need for those additional tools, requiring only a single camera and a simple measurement of the canopy within the observed area. This opens doors for a multitude of exciting applications across various scientific disciplines. For instance, firefighters could deploy camera-equipped drones to generate real-time wind maps during wildfires, significantly improving fire control strategies and firefighter safety. Additionally, this technology has the potential to utilize high-resolution satellite or drone imagery, addressing the critical data gap for accurate near-ground wind speed measurements. This can lead to more precise weather forecasts in sectors like agriculture, aviation, and renewable energy production. In remote locations where wind speed measurement is often challenging and expensive, this method presents a cost-effective solution, enabling wind pattern studies in previously inaccessible areas.

abstractText:
A fundamental question that arises in many fields of mathematics is that of classifying a given collection of objects under study. This amounts to providing a "catalog" or "listing" of these objects, in principle not unlike that of cataloging species in biology or stars and galaxies in astronomy. If such a classification is possible, one has a "complete" understanding of the mathematical structures involved.  Otherwise a more or less "chaotic" behavior is expected. It is thus very important to understand under what circumstances a classification is possible. This difficult foundational question is further complicated by the fact that what constitutes an acceptable classification is very much dependent on the particular field of mathematics studied, so the criteria for a "good" classification in one area might not be appropriate in another.  At its basic level, this project aims to develop a general quantitative theory, which in many situations can precisely measure the complexity of a classification problem and thus provide objective means by which one can decide, in any given field, whether a satisfactory classification of the objects in question is possible. Developments arising in this program often lead to the study of the symmetries of various mathematical structures and their dynamics as well as connections to areas of discrete mathematics, dynamical systems or probability and this is another important aspect of this project. In addition the project also provides research training opportunities for graduate and undergraduate students.

 
The general aim of this project is the development of the theory of definable actions of Polish groups, the structure and classification of their orbit spaces, and the closely related study of definable equivalence relations and graphs. This work is motivated by basic foundational questions, like understanding the nature of complete classification of mathematical objects, up to some notion of equivalence, by invariants, and creating a mathematical framework for measuring the complexity of such classification problems. This theory is developed within the context of descriptive set theory which provides the basic underlying concepts and methods. On the other hand, in view of its broad scope, it has natural interactions with many other areas of mathematics, such as model theory, group theory, topological dynamics, ergodic theory, probability theory and combinatorics. Within this general program Kechris proposes to study: (i) the theory of countable Borel equivalence relations;  (ii) descriptive aspects of the global theory of measure preserving group actions and equivalence relations; (iii) descriptive graph combinatorics, including its relation to ergodic theory, geometric group theory and probability theory; (iv) classification problems for Polish non-archimedean groups; and (v) dynamics of Polish groups.

projectOutComesReport:
The general aim of this project was the development of the theory of definable actions of Polish groups, the structure and classification of their orbit spaces, and the closely related study of definable equivalence relations and graphs. This work is motivated by basic foundational questions, like understanding the nature of complete classification of mathematical objects, up to some notion of equivalence, by invariants, and creating a mathematical framework for measuring the complexity of such classification problems.

 

This theory is developed within the context of descriptive set theory, which provides the basic underlying concepts and methods. On the other hand, in view of its broad scope, it has natural interactions with many other areas of mathematics, such as model theory, computability theory, the theory of topological groups and their representations, topological dynamics, ergodic theory, operator algebras, and combinatorics.

 

Within this general program the PI continued his work on the global theory of ergodic group actions, especially developing a new theory concerning the space of measure preserving equivalence relations and graphs on a standard probability space, culminating in a long manuscript on this subject. The PI also worked extensively in the theory of countable Borel equivalence relations (CBER). With J. Frisch, F. Shinko and Z. Vidnyanszky he initiated the subject of topological realizations of CBERs and with J. Frisch and F. Shinko he studied lifts of actions on quotient spaces of CBERs. Moreover he published a book containing a comprehensive survey of the state of the art in the theory of CBERs. Finally with T. Arant and P. Lutz he developed the theory of Borel graphings of equivalence relations.

 

The project was very well suited for the development of postdoctoral researchers and the training of students both at the undergraduate and graduate level. Although primarily developed within a foundational and set theoretic framework, it interacts strongly with a wide range of subjects in various fields of modern mathematics. Students working in this project had the opportunity to get a broad background in logic and set theory as well as other areas of mathematics. The PI engaged a diverse group of post-doctoral researchers and students, through collaborative work, the Caltech Logic Seminar, as well as topics courses. During the duration of the grant graduate students F. Shinko, J. Frisch and M. Wolman worked with the PI and completed very strong Ph.D. theses, J. Frisch in 2021, F. Shinko in 2022 and M. Wolman in 2025 (expected). Also an undergraduate, E. Jrade worked on a project related to this grant.

 

The PI was actively engaged in broadly disseminating the research supported by the grant through extensive lectures in conferences related to logic and other fields of mathematics. These included: the Chinese Annual Conference on Mathematical Logic, Nankai University; the Erwin Schroedinger Institute Set Theory Workshop, Vienna; the Modern Trends in Operator Algebras Conference, UCLA;  the Workshop on the Frontiers of Set Theory, Fields Institute; the Conference in Descriptive Set Theory and Dynamics, Warsaw; the European Set Theory Colloquium; the conference Model Theory and Groups in Honor of Katrin Tent, Muenster;  the Brin Mathematics Research Center Distinguished Lecture, University of Maryland; the University of Texas Austin Mini-school in Analytic Group Theory, Austin.

 

The PI was also involved in the organization of related programs, meetings and workshops, including: Member of the Scientific Advisory Committee of the thematic program on Set-theoretic Methods in Algebra, Dynamics and Geometry, Fields Institute; Member of the Organizing Committee of the Measurable Combinatorics mini-semester, Budapest.

abstractText:
Many electronic communication systems are bidirectional: they can transmit information in both directions. At any given time, however, the system may only be actively transmitting information in one direction. In this case, the reverse link, which would otherwise be idle, can be used to facilitate transmission in the forward direction. While this fact has long been recognized, it is not well understood how to best employ feedback to maximize the rate and minimize complexity for the forward link. This project will develop practical schemes that improve communication system performance by using feedback links and mathematically characterizing optimal methods for using feedback links. The improved understanding of how to use feedback should improve wireless communication technologies for cellular systems and the internet of things. The project will broaden participation in computing by offering research opportunities to women undergraduates in electrical engineering, with the goal of increasing the number of women who attend graduate programs in the field. It will also develop a publicly-accessible service that provides channels "in the cloud" for digital communication courses and research projects.

Historically, research in information and coding theory has focused on idealized communication scenarios with either perfect feedback or none at all. Many practical systems, however, have feedback links that are available but imperfect. This project will examine how to best use communication channels with a limited amount of feedback to achieve fast and reliable transmission of information. The project will provide clear theoretical guidance about how much feedback information is useful and how the transmitter should use feedback most effectively to adapt its encoding strategy. The project will  provide bounds and approximations on the communication rates and delays achievable with a limited number of feedback transmissions. Leveraging a novel view of feedback coding as a form of joint source-channel coding, the project will address open questions concerning the second-order coding rate and "moderate deviations" performance with feedback. Finally, the project will explore how to improve delay-reliability tradeoffs achievable with feedback in the scenario where an information source, such as a sensor, produces information continuously, by combining the new information with the old information to encode immediately instead of waiting to buffer long blocks of data to encode with traditional block codes.

projectOutComesReport:
This project developed a new information theory of feedback designed to guide the next generation of practical communication systems. Feedback—information sent back from the receiver to the transmitter—has long been known to improve communication, but traditional theory often assumes idealized, unrealistic conditions. In real systems, feedback is limited: messages are short, decoding attempts are infrequent, and feedback signals are simple. Our work created a mathematical foundation that captures these practical constraints and shows how to design systems that make the most of feedback.


Over the course of the award, we advanced the theory along three main directions. First, we studied finite blocklength communication with feedback, where transmissions last only a few hundred channel uses. We developed new bounds and algorithms that optimize how often the receiver should attempt to decode and when feedback should be sent. These results show how limited but well-timed feedback can dramatically reduce delay while maintaining reliability.
Second, we pursued asymptotic analysis to better understand how feedback influences communication as blocklength grows. We clarified its effect on second-order performance of the asymptotic decomposition of the maximum channel rate near channel capacity, providing theoretical insights that can inspire practical design.


Third, we focused on causal information arrivals, which are common in settings like sensor networks and control systems. Instead of waiting to gather large blocks of data, we developed streaming codes that combine newly arriving data with previously transmitted information. Remarkably, we showed that with intelligent feedback-based coding, one can achieve the same performance as classical schemes that assume all data is available in advance. This finding overturns conventional wisdom and opens the door to faster, more responsive communication.


Several major scientific results emerged. We produced new algorithms that optimize variable-length feedback codes, with extensions to multiple access and random access systems—key building blocks of modern wireless networks. We established conditions under which simple linear codes suffice to stabilize dynamical systems observed through noisy channels, and introduced the notion of linear stabilizing capacity, which bridges information theory and control. We also resolved longstanding questions about the capacity of Gaussian channels with feedback and developed a new framework for channels with memory using symmetry reduction from optimization theory, where feedback was essential for simplifying capacity expressions. Beyond feedback itself, we introduced channel skewness, a new fundamental characteristic that governs higher-order behavior in channel coding and improves accuracy in predicting performance at very low error rates.


The project provided extensive opportunities for training and mentorship. Graduate students led many of the theoretical breakthroughs, while undergraduate students made significant contributions to algorithm design, analysis, and publications—some even presenting their work at major international conferences. Several students received recognition for their research, including best paper award nominations, and one student’s work led to a patent application. Alumni of the project have gone on to faculty positions and advanced graduate studies, demonstrating the project’s role in developing the next generation of scientific leaders.


The broader impacts are substantial. Our theory and algorithms directly inform the design of communication systems where feedback is constrained, such as the Internet of Things, real-time control over wireless links, and sensor networks. By showing when and how feedback can be used most effectively, the project contributes to faster, more reliable, and more energy-efficient communication technologies. In addition, the integration of undergraduate researchers and the dissemination of results through talks, preprints, and journal publications expanded the reach of the project to both the academic community and future practitioners.


In sum, this project reshaped our understanding of feedback in communication. The outcomes—spanning new mathematical theories, algorithms, and applications—advance both the intellectual foundations of information theory and its real-world relevance, while training students at multiple levels in cutting-edge research.

abstractText:
Scientists investigate the generation and evolution of magma (molten rock) with a range of tools such as field-based studies, experiments at high pressures and temperatures, and models of the physical and chemical behavior of partially molten rocks. The modeling component is particularly important for situations where field work is too hazardous or inaccessible and where it would take too many experiments to fully describe the processes leading to a catastrophic volcanic eruption. This work focuses on continuing development of a flexible, powerful, and easy-to-use package of modeling software used by hundreds of Earth scientists. The alphaMELTS 2 software can model complex scenarios with changing pressure, temperature, and chemical composition while monitoring energy and mass of major and trace elements and gaseous species. This project will increase the mineral systems alphaMELTS 2 can model, support users, extend applications of the software in teaching and training, and facilitate outreach workshops to train new users. These workshops will reach several dozen users, mostly early-career scientists, and equip them with quantitative tools for modern petrology research.

There are several particular advances on which this effort will focus, mostly new thermodynamic model calibrations for use with alphaMELTS 2 and related tools: modeling of CO2 in mantle magmatic systems; the amphibole mineral group; the biotite mineral group; more flexible treatment of trace elements; better integration with MATLAB, Python, and other development environments; and user interaction and training through the online forum and dedicated training workshops. Extension of the calibration strategy to exploit new categories of experiments such as two-liquid equilibria, will allow the pMELTS code for high-pressure melting to describe carbon-bearing systems such as subducted carbonate or upwelling carbonated mantle rocks. The most widespread and important igneous minerals that are not well-modeled in current generations of MELTS are amphibole and biotite; a new strategy will be implemented that can tackle the great complexity of naturally occurring amphiboles and make an accurate yet tractable calibration. Dynamically loadable libraries that allow for seamless incorporation of all alphaMELTS 2 functionality into any Fortran, C++, Matlab or Python code will enable coupling with other codes and flexible scripting. Finally, a large expansion of the phases and trace elements that can be treated with variable and modular partition coefficients will allow users to customize their trace element calculations for greater accuracy.

projectOutComesReport:
Igneous petrology, the study of rocks formed by cooling of magma, addresses problems including the temperature and composition of the Earth's interior over time, volcanic hazards, the formation of magmatic ore deposits, and more. Scientists working in this area collect field and laboratory observations but they depend on computational models to test their data against hypotheses, because igneous processes occur at depth in the Earth, where we cannot observe them directly. The accuracy and ease-of-use of available computational models is therefore a key limiting factor in scientific progress and discovery of new knowledge in this area (as in many other fields). This Geoinformatics award funded the ongoing development, maintenance, and user support of a software package we call alphaMELTS, which enables the US and world scientific community to predict the outcomes of complex geological processes involving the melting of rocks and crystallization of magma. The "facility" award recognized that there were already several hundred users of the software; as we finish the award the user base has grown further, with frequent new downloads and a steady stream of publications citing the software.

Some of our work under this project focused on aspects of software engineering and maintenance, such as keeping up with changing operating systems and chipsets or migrating from proprietary software to entirely open-source software. Another aspect of our work centered on supporting users by answering their questions, debugging their installations, or suggesting the best ways to model the problems they were trying to solve. Over the four-year span of the award, we hosted numerous workshops to train users — ranging from undergraduate students to senior scientists — in how to install and use the alphaMELTS and related software packages. In turn many of these attendees put the software to work in their own publications, maximizing the impact of this project in moving the scientific enterprise forwards.

The supported work was not just software development, maintenance, and distribution, however. We also worked on extending the model by adding new chemical components (e.g. CO2) or more complete descriptions of minerals (notably the amphibole group), and we applied the model ourselves in a series of papers focusing on various problems in igneous and economic geology. We focused especially on the igneous rocks of the Arabian-Nubian Shield, which outcrops in Egypt and Saudi Arabia and hosts a series of metal-rich igneous intrusions and volcanic provinces that are not easily explained by conventional plate tectonic processes.

Several PhD students were supported by this award and completed or made progress towards their degrees thanks to their research, which in turn contributed to improving or applying the alphaMELTS software.

abstractText:
In almost every field of science, it is now possible to capture large amounts of data. This has led machine learning to play an increasingly important role in scientific discovery, for example sifting through large amounts of data to identify interesting events. But modern machine learning techniques are less well suited for the critical tasks of devising hypotheses consistent with the data or imagining new experiments to test those hypotheses. The goal of this Expeditions project is to develop new learning techniques that can help automate this process of generating scientific theories from data. In order to ground this research in real applications, the project focuses on four domains where these techniques can have the most significant impact: organic chemistry, RNA splicing, cognitive and behavioral science, and computing systems. Machine learning is already demonstrating value in all of these domains, including predicting properties of organic compounds, recognizing complex social activities, and modeling the performance of computer systems. However, the proposed techniques could have a transformative impact in all of these domains by helping scientists gain a deeper understanding of the processes that give rise to their data. This deeper understanding could lead to important contributions ranging from more efficient drug discovery to improved teaching methods grounded on a better understanding of cognition. 

To realize this vision, the project will develop new methods for learning neurosymbolic models that combine neural elements capable of identifying complex patterns in data with symbolic constructs that are able to represent higher level concepts. The approach is based on the observation that programming languages provide a uniquely expressive formalism to describe complex models. The aim is therefore to develop learning techniques that can produce models that look more like the models that scientists already write by hand in code. These neurosymbolic techniques will more easily incorporate prior knowledge about the phenomena being modeled, and produce interpretable models that can be analyzed to devise new experiments or to infer causal relations. By developing these techniques and building them into tools that can be used by scientists in a variety of fields, this project has the potential to revolutionize the way scientific knowledge is derived from data. More broadly, these new techniques will be useful in any setting that requires learning more interpretable models with strong requirements on their desired behavior.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The overarching objective of this Expeditions project is to develop foundational methods for neurosymbolic learning—integrating the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks with the compositional structure and interpretability of symbolic reasoning. These hybrid models can significantly advance the automation of scientific discovery by enabling systems that are not only data-driven but also guided by formal representations of domain knowledge. At the core of our research is the view that programming languages offer a uniquely expressive framework for encoding high-level scientific models. By enabling learning algorithms to produce interpretable programs—rather than opaque statistical models—we aim to create systems that mirror the way human scientists construct and reason about complex phenomena.

PI Yue's foundational contributions to this effort have focused on establishing the theoretical foundations of neurosymbolic programming, developing novel algorithms that bridge neural and symbolic learning, and demonstrating their transformative potential across scientific domains—with particular emphasis on behavioral analysis and autonomous systems. His work has created a unified framework that combines the flexibility of neural networks with the interpretability and formal guarantees of symbolic reasoning, enabling new capabilities in scientific discovery and safety-critical applications.

In establishing the theoretical foundations of neurosymbolic programming, PI Yue co-authored the comprehensive survey Neurosymbolic Programming (Foundations and Trends in Programming Languages, 2021) with co-PIs Chaudhuri and Solar-Lezama, along with collaborators Ellis, Polozov, and Singh. This foundational work systematically categorized the landscape of neurosymbolic approaches, analyzing how neural and symbolic components can be combined to achieve benefits over pure deep learning—including improved interpretability, sample efficiency, generalization, and the ability to incorporate prior knowledge. The framework has become a standard reference in the field, providing the conceptual foundation for subsequent algorithmic developments and applications across the project.

In developing core algorithmic innovations, PI Yue led the creation of Learning Differentiable Programs with Admissible Neural Heuristics (NeurIPS 2020), which introduced a novel approach to program synthesis that uses neural networks to guide combinatorial search. This method learns programs from data by relaxing discrete programs into differentiable forms that can be optimized end-to-end, with the training loss serving as an admissible heuristic for guiding symbolic search. This breakthrough enabled efficient learning of interpretable programs from limited data, directly supporting the project's vision of combining neural learning with symbolic structure. The approach has been applied successfully to tasks ranging from list manipulation to image classification, demonstrating its generality.

For scientific applications, PI Yue supervised and co-authored a comprehensive body of work demonstrating neurosymbolic programming's transformative potential in behavioral analysis. In Task Programming (CVPR 2021, Best Student Paper Award), his group introduced TREBA, a framework where domain experts encode knowledge through simple programs that define auxiliary learning tasks, achieving 10× annotation efficiency improvements for mouse behavior classification. This was extended in AutoSWAP (CVPR 2022), which automatically synthesizes labeling functions through program synthesis, and in the development of neurosymbolic encoders (TMLR 2022), which compose neural networks with symbolic programs from domain-specific languages to learn interpretable representations. PI Yue also supervised the development of B-KinD (CVPR 2022) and BKinD-3D (CVPR 2023) for self-supervised keypoint discovery in 2D and 3D, demonstrating that meaningful structure can be discovered automatically without manual annotations across diverse organisms.

abstractText:
Island arcs are chains of volcanic islands that form at subduction zone plate boundaries where one plate is being dragged beneath another, recycling old crust to the Earth’s mantle and creating new continental crust through volcanism. A central question surrounding these systems is whether processes that occur deeply in the subduction zone affect processes that are observed on the surface. This is especially debated for what drives surface uplift and related island arc exhumation and erosion. Uplift and exhumation of island arcs in other localities have been attributed to a variety of factors, from deep tectonic drivers to climate-surface interactions, with exhumation rates and erosion estimates that vary by orders of magnitude. In many locations, the arc exhumation history is difficult to study because it may be overprinted by later thermal or physical processes. The Aleutian Arc is unique in that it includes over 50 islands composed of both active and inactive volcanoes over 1,900 miles from Alaska to Russia, and has limited overprinting by secondary events. In addition, it has a volcanic history that spans 50 million years, so that the ancient magma chambers of past volcanoes are now exposed on the islands’ surfaces today. These plutonic rocks hold a record of past island uplift, exhumation, and erosion that can address key questions regarding: When were the Aleutians uplifted? When and how much has been eroded through time? Was uplift and subsequent erosion constant or cyclical? How does it vary geographically along the length of the arc? Specifically, the answers to these questions will shed light on the link between plate-scale processes and uplift; the timing and magnitude of erosion, contributing sediment and geochemical inputs to North Pacific; and the relationship between plutonic exhumation rates, geochemistry, and emplacement depth. The Aleutians have functioned as a natural laboratory to test fundamental principles regarding subduction zone evolution for more than four decades. This study will make a novel contribution to the existing extensive geochemical and geodynamic research. In terms of Broader Impacts, this award supports a new PI and engages underrepresented minority students and teachers, from the undergraduate through K-12 level. 

	In order to quantify when and by how much the Aleutians experienced surface uplift and erosion, plutonic samples from ~10 islands that span 870 miles of arc length will be analyzed for emplacement depth and subsequent uplift rates. This work will place the exhumation history of the Central Aleutians in the context of 1) driving forces involving regional tectonics and subduction zone processes; and 2) geochemical inputs to the N. Pacific via erosion of arc material. In order to answer these questions, previously sampled and well-characterized plutonic rocks from across the central Aleutians will be characterized by pluton crystallization age, emplacement depth, and 2 or more thermochronometers with different thermal sensitivities (e.g., apatite and/or zircon, (U-Th)/He and/or fission track). Thermochronology techniques, particularly the use of multiple chronometers with different temperature sensitivities within the same sample, can constrain exhumation rates and be used to estimate erosion rates over time. Coupling the thermochronological data with emplacement depth will help constrain the amount of material eroded over that time. The timing and geographic trends revealed by these data can then be related in time and space to previously proposed drivers for uplift, including plate rotation, change in convergence angle and rate, or the development of an accretionary prism.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The primary intellectual goals of this project were to quantify the exhumation history (or the timing of vertical movement of rocks through the crust) of magmatic rocks from the Central Aleutians islands through collaborative research between USC and Caltech. Understanding the exhumation history of the Aleutian arc will help constrain the link between tectonic plate-scale processes and island uplift and provide better information on the timing and magnitude of erosion, which contributed sediments into the northern Pacific. The primary contribution of research from Caltech researchers was to understand how deep within the crust the magmatic rocks initially crystallized. This was accomplished through studying the chemistry of the minerals amphibole, biotite, and plagioclase, which are sensitive to the pressure and temperatures of crystallization. Co-PI Bucholz recruited and mentored an undergraduate intern from UCSB for 10 weeks during the summer of 2021 to lead this analytical endeavor. The internship involved examining the rocks with an optical microscope and then using electron probe microanalytical techniques to obtain the mineral compositions. Crystallization depths for seven different magmatic intrusions (using 14 samples) from five different islands were obtained.           

            The primary broader impact goal for this project was to integrate research and mentorship for graduate and undergraduate students from under-represented minority groups and to support their professional development. The PIs at Caltech and USC both mentored a female URM graduate student at USC through regular meetings to discuss sample preparation and planned analyses and supported her attendance at conferences. Co-PI Bucholz mentored a female URM undergraduate from UCSB during the summer of 2021 and discussed graduate school opportunities and career paths with her. After graduation from UCSB, the undergraduate chose to pursue a PhD in Earth Sciences.

abstractText:
Many goals motivate scientific interest in human memory. The brain's ability to create, store, and access memories helps enable vision, speech, learning, thought, and identity; understanding memory elucidates both the functions of remembering and the functions that rely on them. Injury and illness can suppress or overstimulate memory function, with extreme cases causing ailments like Alzheimer's disease and dementia on the one hand and PTSD and addiction on the other; a theory explaining how biological mechanisms create memory phenomena may help pinpoint the mechanistic changes responsible for memory failures. This project outlines a path to a fundamentally new theory for how the microscopic behavior of individual neurons generates the macroscopic phenomena of memory performance. The potential outcomes of this project can shed greater light on the understanding of human memory and the processes that influence it.

This project seeks to create models for brain behavior and memory phenomena and applies mathematical tools to investigate whether the brain model can generate those memory phenomena. Brain behavior is structured here as a Markov process derived from models of individual neurons, their connectivity, and stimuli. Markov processes, which capture the assumption that the past affects the future only through its effects on the present, exhibit a characteristic behavior called stochastic convergence, where the Markov process trends toward a predictable steady-state behavior over time. The memory model seeks to capture memory retrieval, formation, and storage as phenomena where the brain state converges to desired outcomes under corresponding stimuli, creates new convergence relationships through neuronal plasticity, and protects old convergence relationships from damage caused by that same plasticity.

projectOutComesReport:
This project, funded under the National Science Foundation's EArly-Concept Grants for Exploratory Research (EAGER) program, invented and developed new mathematical tools to help us understand how the brain creates, stores, and retrieves memories.  The work built on prior results from the field of neuroscience that provide mathematical models for the behavior of individual neurons, trace the map of connections between individual neurons and the brain regions into which they are organized, and demonstrate the performance of humans on a variety of memory tasks under a wide range of settings and constraints.  The challenge addressed under the grant was to build tools that help us determine whether and how neurons that behave according to prior models and are connected in the ways described in the literature can achieve the types of memory performance observed in the experimental research literature.  

Intellectual Merit:  Three central outcomes from this work are described briefly below.  

  • The work done under this proposal developed new mathematical models of the phenomena of memory creation, storage, and retrieval.  While models of individual neurons capture how each neuron behaves in response to conditions in its environment (such as how each neuron reacts when some of the neurons that influence it "fire"), they do not describe how that behavior creates the phenomena of memory.  For example, they do not describe how we learn the names of people we meet, how the brain protects memories that it stored previously from the changes need to learn new names, or how we retrieve names that we already know.  The models created under this grant proposed new solutions to the question of how neurons work together to create, store, and retrieve memories.
  • In order to understand whether and how the model of individual neuron behavior and the map of neuron connectivity work together to generate the phenomena of memory as captured by the newly proposed models, the work funded by this grant also developed mathematical tools for describing how the behavior of individual neurons and the networks through which they interact evolve over time in response to different stimuli.  The tools developed in this work are related to a mathematical theory that describes how certain sequences of individually unpredictable events (called "Markov chains") become more predictable when viewed over time. While the behaviors of individual neurons and networks of these neurons are not well-modeled as Markov chains, the work funded by this grant proved that they are related to Markov chains in a way that makes them similarly predictable; sequences that were found to be predictable in this way were named "Markov-adjacent" sequences.  
  • Combining the new memory models with the new theory of Markov-adjacent sequences enabled a new understanding of how stable behavior can arise in the brain's reaction to a world characterized by seemingly endless variety and change.  This stability is critical for understanding how the macroscopic behavior of memory phenomena can arise from the microscopic behavior of individual neurons and their connections. 

Broader Impact:  While the primary aim of this project was to answer the important questions of how the brain creates, stores, and retrieves memories, the results derived in this work may also have impact in a broader range of problems.  Three examples follow.  

  • The type of stable behavior proposed in this work to be critical to the performance of memory tasks and demonstrated to arise from the brain model may also be useful for understanding other brain functions.  For example, the human brain is extremely efficient at understanding visual information. The same mathematical tools that help us understand how we can reliably retrieve memories may also help us understand how we can recognize objects we see even as viewing angles, lighting conditions, and surrounding scenery change.  
  • The mathematical tools created to understand healthy brain function may also be useful for understanding how the brain behaves more broadly.  For example, understanding how changing the neuron model changes the full-brain behavior that arises may be helpful in understanding and tackling neuro-degenerative diseases that affect the behavior of individual neurons. Likewise, understanding how changing the connectivity map changes the full-brain behavior that arises may be helpful in understanding and tackling challenges faced after certain brain injuries.  
  • The theory of Markov-adjancent sequences may be useful beyond the study of neuroscience.  For example, it may be useful for modeling how economic markets behave over time or how to better predict phenomena like earthquakes or weather.

abstractText:
Among the unsolved mysteries of Earth’s history are the age of the first continental crust and whether processes akin to the modern plate tectonic cycle are required to form continental crust. The oldest preserved minerals found on Earth are zircons up to 4.4 billion years old, which is only a few tens of million years younger than the Earth itself. Some geochemists interpret these zircons as evidence that there was already, at that time, crust similar to continents, but it is very unclear how and whether plate tectonics could have started so early. In this work the investigators will explore an alternative series of processes that operated only in this early era of Earth history and determine whether these processes could have led to the formation of continental crust and could explain the zircon evidence. The process to be studied is rapid changes in the Earth’s rotation rate, or length of day. This is motivated by the most successful theories of the origin of the Moon, which all involve a giant impact, perhaps with a Mars-sized object, that left the Earth molten and rapidly spinning and ejected debris that condensed to form a very close-in Moon. It only takes about a million years for the outer shell of the Earth to freeze and become rigid, forming a crust and lithosphere (a crust that would be, at this stage, nothing like continents). It is well-understood that, over the next ten million years or so (and continuing at an ever-decreasing rate all the way to the present), the enormous tides raised by such a close moon cause a gravitational interaction that slows the Earth’s rotation and boosts the Moon to a higher orbit. What has not been studied in detail is the consequence of this for the shape of the Earth itself and for the deformation experienced by the rocky outer shell of the Earth as it changes shape. A rapidly spinning planet flattens significantly into a shape with a large equatorial bulge so that just after the Moon formed, the radius of the Earth through the equator may have been twice as large as that through the poles. As the length of day increases and the equatorial diameter decreases, this puts the entire equatorial region into a state of compressive stress that will thicken the lithosphere, driving possibly water-bearing material (that has interacted with the steam-rich early atmosphere) to depths where it undergoes another stage of melting, the products of which should resemble continental crust. In order to study these phenomena in detail, investigators will create a series of computer codes necessary to describe rapidly rotating planets and the melting and crystallization processes they experience. The team will document and release these codes to the scientific community for use in numerous other studies. They also intend to develop educational and outreach resources based on the unique and dramatic series of events that our planet experienced at its birth. This work will involve advanced scientific and professional training for a postdoctoral scholar as well as undergraduate research experiences.

The numerical models that will be used to explore the consequences of rotational evolution on the early Earth include HERCULES, alphaMELTS, Perple_X, and custom advection-diffusion codes. HERCULES solves the hydrostatic equations of planetary structure in a frame that does not assume spherical symmetry or small perturbations thereto. It is able to accurately describe pressure, density, and gravity in a planet with arbitrarily fast rotation rate up to its stability limit (where angular acceleration at the equator exactly cancels gravity). HERCULES will be improved for this project to incorporate a wider range of equations of state. Extents of melting as a function of latitude and the composition and thickness of proto-crust will then be computed in the structures predicted by HERCULES using the pMELTS calibration, implemented in alphaMELTS for MATLAB or Python (tools developed with NSF geoinformatics support). The next stage is to move from statics to dynamics and calculate deformation rates and mechanisms using tectonophysics codes that incorporate elastic-plastic rheologies, brittle failure and viscous flow.  Knowing the type of faults that are predicted and the amplitude of motion, the investigators can describe the pressure-temperature paths that protocrustal material will experience using advection-diffusion models. Finally, along those P-T paths Perplex_X pseudosections will be utilized to predict where felsic melts will form and whether the resulting crust will be buoyantly stable and likely to survive long enough to be eroded at the surface and create detrital zircons.
